header: Date: 2026-09-30 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52 minutes | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (AtlasFin - Head of ML), Sofia Martinez (AtlasFin - Platform Eng), Evan Liu (AtlasFin - SRE)
summary: POC scoping call to align on benchmark planning and harness integration. Covered success criteria, workload sizing, streaming vs non-streaming tests, customer scripts, security/VPC constraints, and timeline for a 2-week benchmark run. Agreed next steps and assigned owners.
topics: Load testing plan: streaming vs non-streaming
Networking and security constraints (VPC, KMS, audit logs)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'll kick us off — this is a POC scoping call focused on benchmark harness integration. Quick intro, then Liam will walk through the harness and we can go into streaming vs non-streaming tests.
[00:18] Raj: Yep, thanks. We wanted to confirm scope — we're trying to validate cost and latency for our core inference workload, roughly 250 RPS average with 400ms payloads, and spikes to 800 RPS during batch windows.
[00:34] Liam: Got it. Quick clarifying question — when you say payloads, are these short-form prompts or longer multi-turn chat?
[00:45] Raj: Primarily single-turn scoring for risk models, so prompts are around 150 tokens, but we also have a small chat path for alerts that can go to ~600 tokens. Mostly non-streaming, but alerts would benefit from streaming.
[01:05] Sofia: Also FYI, we run in our VPC and will need to test the private deployment path. We do have a SOC2 requirement and an internal KMS.
[01:18] Maya: Good call. We'll include both hosted and private paths in the plan. For success criteria, can you state what "pass" looks like? Latency SLOs, cost threshold, and functional accuracy?
[01:32] Raj: Passing is p95 < 450ms for the scoring path, p99 < 1.2s during average load, and cost per 1M tokens below our target — ballpark $X (we'll give the exact number offline). Accuracy: outputs must match our current model within defined regression tolerance — we have eval scripts.
[01:50] Liam: Great — that maps cleanly to bench metrics: latency by percentile, throughput, tokens/sec, and regression tests against your eval set. We'll hook the harness to run your scripts for the functional checks.
[02:06] Evan: On the load shape — those spikes are predictable, about 15-20 minute bursts twice a day. We'll share traces. Also we want tail-latency during spikes measured end-to-end, including network and ingress.
[02:20] Maya: Perfect, please send a week's trace and a sample of the scripts. For harness options — we have two recommended flows: 1) non-streaming batch runner that replays requests at target RPS and 2) streaming runner for low-latency token streaming tests.
[02:36] Raj: What's the difference operationally? Does streaming increase cost?
[02:41] Liam: Streaming tends to increase overhead in small increments — more connections and longer-lived streams — but it reduces time-to-first-token. For some models the per-token efficiency is similar, for others streaming can be slightly more expensive if it prevents batching. We'll quantify in the estimates.
[02:57] Sofia: For the private path, our network team needs to know port ranges and peering windows. We also have strict egress rules.
[03:05] Maya: We'll include a connectivity matrix in the repo. Liam, can you call out the required ports and IP ranges?
[03:11] Liam: Sure — we'll provide a minimal set. Typically HTTPS 443 plus a small ephemeral range for the streaming sockets; we'll put exact CIDR ranges in the doc.
[03:22] Raj: On the harness side — how hard is it to plug in our existing runner? We have a Python-based load generator that emits requests identical to prod.
[03:30] Liam: That's the ideal case. The harness accepts a pluggable client adapter — Python script or a simple REST wrapper. We can run your scripts as-is or adapt a thin shim to conform to our result collectors.
[03:42] Evan: We also need metrics exported to our Prometheus stack. Can the harness push or expose metrics?
[03:48] Liam: Yes — it can push Prometheus metrics or push metrics to a file/HTTP endpoint. We usually ship a small exporter shim if you want to scrape from your Prom stack.
[03:58] Maya: Let's talk timeline — what's your target for completing the POC and making a decision?
[04:03] Raj: We'd like a 2-week benchmark window followed by a week to review results — target decision in late October, so start tests around 2026-10-12.
[04:13] Maya: That fits — we'll aim to have the harness ready and a kickoff load test in the week of Oct 11.
[04:20] Raj: Cool. For success criteria we also need reproducibility. Can we pin model versions and quantization profiles in the harness?
[04:29] Liam: Yes, the harness config supports model pins, quantization settings, batch sizes, and concurrency. We'll add an explicit field for kernel and quant flags so we can reproduce runs.
[04:38] Sofia: Any gotchas on the streaming tests? We worry about breakage if the client disconnects mid-stream.
[04:44] Liam: We'll add retry and connection drop simulations as part of the harness. Also we'll instrument to capture partial outputs.
[04:51] Raj: On security — we need audit logs for requests and key rotations with our KMS. How does Redwood handle that in Private mode?
[04:58] Maya: In Private we integrate with customer KMS and forward audit logs to your syslog/S3 — we'll share the security pack. For hosted we have exportable audit trails but can't integrate your KMS.
[05:12] Evan: SSO and RBAC? We'll need SAML for the console and API keys for automated runs.
[05:18] Maya: SAML works for console; for the harness we recommend scoped API keys with restricted permissions. We'll document key best practices in the repo.
[05:26] Raj: Back to workload sizing — our p95 target is 450ms but what's realistic for the private GPU types? We might use A100 or H100 variants.
[05:36] Liam: H100 will give better throughput for big models; A100 is often cheaper per-hour. We'll run both and report normalized tokens/sec and cost per 1M tokens. Provide your model size and we can recommend quantization and kernel flags.
[05:50] Sofia: We also plan to run a controlled degradation test — stepping down model size to see quality/cost tradeoffs. Can harness support that?
[05:57] Liam: Yep — harness can automate multi-config runs and produce comparison dashboards.
[06:03] Raj: On metrics — we need p50/p95/p99, tokens per second, cost per 1M tokens, and regression pass/fail. Anything else?
[06:11] Maya: Also success/failure counts, retry rates, connection churn, and memory/GPU utilization if we run on Dedicated. We'll capture those as part of the runner.
[06:21] Evan: Can agents capture KV cache warmup behavior? Our workloads have prefix reuse so warm cache matters.
[06:28] Liam: We'll include warmup phases in the harness and measure cold vs warm latencies. We'll provide a script to replay sessions to emulate KV hit-rates.
[06:37] Raj: For the regression tests, we have an eval harness — can we point the benchmark to call our eval endpoints?
[06:44] Liam: Yes, either call your eval endpoints or execute local eval scripts and compare outputs. We'll support both; if you can send eval scripts that is ideal.
[06:51] Maya: Small note — transcription: sorry just thinking aloud — on the hosted route if latency is slightly higher, we can recommend Dedicated for the test to show best-case tail-latency.
[07:03] Raj: That makes sense. If Dedicated lowers p99 we want to know the delta vs hosted and cost delta.
[07:09] Liam: We'll produce a delta report: hosted vs dedicated vs private (your private infra).
[07:16] Sofia: For the private tests, our SOC2 team will want to review network flows and the audit trail. Can you share SOC2 documentation?
[07:24] Maya: Absolutely — I'll attach the security pack and SOC2 attestation in the next email.
[07:30] Evan: One operational constraint: we can only allow peering during a 2-hour maintenance window on Tuesdays/Thursdays. That might push the test schedule a bit.
[07:38] Maya: Noted — we'll aim to schedule the heavy load windows within those windows for private tests.
[07:45] Raj: On failure modes — if a model fallback happens, can the harness detect and log it? We use automatic rollbacks in prod and need to be sure the bench won't conflate fallbacks with lower latency runs.
[07:56] Liam: The harness logs model version per-request and will flag any fallbacks. We'll include a flag to block fallbacks if you want a strict run.
[08:05] Maya: Any blockers from the customer side today?
[08:08] Raj: We'll just need to gather traces and eval scripts; otherwise sounds good. We'll also confirm the $$ cost target offline.
[08:15] Sofia: We'll check the peering windows and confirm dates by Friday.
[08:19] Evan: I'll pull SLOs and the exact p99 numbers and post them to the shared doc.
[08:24] Maya: Great — to recap: we'll share the harness repo and runner templates; you'll provide traces, eval scripts, and peering windows; and we'll schedule a load-test kickoff the week of Oct 11.
[08:36] Raj: Perfect. A couple of quick technical clarifications: 1) will the harness simulate client-side backpressure? 2) can we run multiple concurrent configs?
[08:44] Liam: 1) yes, we simulate backpressure and network jitter; 2) yes, the harness supports parallel experiment runs with reproducible seeds.
[08:52] Maya: I'll also include a quick-run checklist — minimal sample, full-week sample, and network checklist.
[08:59] Raj: Last question — any integrations with our cost-monitoring tools? We run internal cost dashboards.
[09:05] Liam: We can export a CSV and push to S3; we also have a small adapter to push to common cost services. If you share the schema, we can map fields.
[09:15] Sofia: OK thanks, we'll follow up with details.
[09:18] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll send the security pack, harness link, and proposed kickoff times after this call.
[09:24] Raj: Thanks, bye.
[09:26] (call ends)
notes: Customer prioritized p95/p99 latency and cost per 1M tokens as primary success criteria
Agreed to run both streaming and non-streaming benchmarks; harness supports adapters for customer scripts
Private deployment requires VPC peering windows (2-hour maintenance windows) and KMS integration
Reproducibility addressed via model pins, quant flags, and harness config snapshots
Action items assigned to both Redwood and AtlasFin with target dates
